problems.rationale: The mathematics is settled; the blocker is proof-engineering volume: Cook's glider catalogue and collision table can be kernel-checked piece by piece within a month, but the compiler bisimulation and the glider-calculus noninterference argument are the long pole and no approach plausibly finishes them in 30 days. Over a year, a staged route (table audit, then kernel-checked collisions, then cyclic-tag universality, then the composition) is credible given agents' steady Lean throughput, but kernel cost without native_decide and timing bookkeeping could stall it. A logged Lean report covering layers 1 to 3 with a clean axiom audit would move me up substantially. The 30-day number is below the best approach product on purpose: that approach (cyclic-tag universality without Rule 110) settles only a piece and cannot meet the acceptance criteria alone.

approaches.note: Full chain to the universality theorem is months of proof engineering; layers 1 to 3 in a month is plausible but does not count as completion.
Simulation audit is routine code, but extracting the exact gap ranges from Cook's paper unambiguously is the risk the proposer names.
The grammar-inference step for tile arrangements is research with no existing description, so completion is very unlikely in a month.
Same end-to-end refinement burden as the other full formalizations, without a staged fallback.
Independent reconstruction plus Lean replay of every trace is larger than a pure audit, and bounded search leaves completeness open.
Kernel-checking each published collision is finite and well scoped, but transcription and blocked kernel reduction of long collisions may not all fit in a month.
Tag-system and cyclic-tag simulation is classical, CA-free and well suited to Lean, though the Cocke–Minsky encoding has fiddly bookkeeping.
Depends on the two other modules existing first, and the proposer itself expects the bisimulation not to finish in a month.

problems.rationale: Either direction needs new mathematics: a decidability invariant for machine 596440 on eventually periodic tapes or a periodic-background construction, and none of the approaches shows how an agent finds it. The search and census approaches will complete but, by their own failure signatures, exhaustion does not settle the question. Only a surprising positive search hit (a periodic-background emulator) or a uniform regular invariant appearing in the census would move me. The 30-day number is below the best approach product on purpose: the non-periodicity lemma for Smith's tape settles a sub-question and does not meet either acceptance route.

approaches.note: Porting bbchallenge-style deciders to non-halting observables is new work, and the census fallback is likely but rarely decisive.
Implementing and instrumenting Smith's whole emulation chain is large and the gadget search space is probably too big.
Formalizing a roughly 40-page chain plus a tape-complexity theorem is far beyond a month.
The bounded search will likely run, but a negative result falsifies only the searched family and a positive hit is improbable.
The bounded-crossing lemma is an unknown global invariant; experiments cannot supply it.
Non-periodicity of Smith's tape is a modest lemma, but the axiom audit depends on a public Lean development whose state is not in the slice and is unverified.
Requires a finite invariant no one knows to exist, proved for all periods and centers.
A fixed-grammar simulation sweep is straightforward to run, but exhaustion is explicitly non-settling and acceptance is unlikely.

problems.rationale: This is an open problem since 2002; a positive answer needs a conditional data-reading reaction among Rule 54 gliders that nobody has found, and a negative answer needs a conservation law or decomposition theorem with no known candidate. Catalogue completeness and collision censuses are very likely to be produced and are useful, but the falsifier says partial results leave the problem open. A census that turns up a conditional-append reaction would move me sharply. The 30-day number is below the best approach product on purpose: the bounded catalogue-completeness theorem settles only its own piece, and the falsifiers say partial results leave the problem open.

approaches.note: Catalogue and collision table are computable, but synthesis of a full CTS emulation is unlikely and the negative fallback is bounded only.
The decomposition theorem and potential function are unknown mathematics, and success covers only finite seeds.
De Bruijn cycle enumeration reduces to finite graphs, so a bounded completeness certificate is feasible, though Lean-checking large certificates by kernel may be slow.
SAT spacetime synthesis of phase-restoring modules is ambitious and failure does not prove non-universality.
Needs a finite particle quotient that is not known to exist, then a Lean proof of closure.
A pairwise collision census to separation 256 with two simulators is routine compute; the gate-set search is the uncertain part.
No published conservation law of this strength; the proposer concedes the swarm lacks the theorem.
Kernel-checking the 2006 gates is feasible, but proving the generated monoid cannot store a work string is a real algebra problem.

problems.rationale: The three prize statements are far out of reach (well under 0.02), so nearly all probability sits on the weaker acceptance route: a conditional non-periodicity theorem with an explicit hypothesis (Jen's two-column theorem formalized and extended) or a period lower bound exceeding computational checks. Jen in Lean is plausible within a month, and whether reviewers count it as the 'new' conditional result is the main uncertainty; a certified period bound beyond the published billion-bit horizon needs either large GPU time or a Lean replay that is too slow. The restricted-model DFAO lower bounds are likely to complete but do not obviously match the acceptance wording, which is why my 30-day number sits below that approach's product (the validator warning is kept deliberately).

approaches.note: Jen's theorem via left-permutivity is formalizable, but the decisive result also needs a new conditional theorem about the center column.
About 10^4 GPU-hours is not clearly available to the swarm; if run, the period exclusion and density test are definite.
SAT plus verified DRAT checking for small-state DFAOs is a finite, tool-supported task, though the Lean link to the checker adds work.
SAT encoding of the light cone scales badly, so certified bounds exceeding existing computational checks are doubtful.
Requires a currently unknown invariant linking global permutivity to the single seeded column.
Blocked Lean replay past a published horizon of billions of steps is likely too slow for the kernel in a month.
Equidistribution of a single explicit orbit is precisely the open prize step.
A finite prefix bounds kernel size but cannot prove infinitely many distinct kernel sequences, so the full non-automaticity proof needs an idea.

problems.rationale: The n = 3 enumeration is tractable with numerical witnesses plus exact rational verification, but certifying incapability for every remaining pattern (CAD or nlsat per pattern) and proving a necessary-and-sufficient sign-pattern theorem are both required, and the theorem is the blocker. A clean empirical census that reveals a simple combinatorial boundary would make the theorem much more reachable over a year. Mathlib's lack of Routh–Hurwitz adds friction but n = 3 coefficient conditions can be proved directly. The 30-day number is below the best approach product on purpose: the n = 2 and equal-diffusion theorems and the n = 4 Monte Carlo are pieces; the criteria need an n = 3 necessary-and-sufficient theorem.

approaches.note: The conjectured characterization may not be the right one, and Lean needs Routh–Hurwitz infrastructure first.
Witness search is easy; exact incapability certificates for the residual patterns and the n = 4 table are the uncertain part.
The embedding lemma is plausible, but counting non-sign-stable patterns with a rate is a real proof and eigenvalue perturbation is thin in Mathlib.
CAD over thousands of patterns is feasible-ish, but translating certificates into Lean is the stated missing piece.
Sampling to n = 8 will run, but it cannot settle the almost-all conjecture by itself.
Two classical results with short proofs; equal-diffusion impossibility is linear algebra Mathlib can handle.
Sampling finds capable witnesses easily, but covering certificates for every incapable pattern are harder than the plan suggests.
A Monte Carlo of 2000 patterns with a pre-registered 0.9 threshold is cheap and will give a definite interval for n = 4.

problems.rationale: This is the most formalizable problem in the slice: the regression identity, the additive-fitness theorem and a synergistic counterexample are finite-population algebra that Lean plus Mathlib's Finset sums can do, and several approaches target exactly the acceptance criteria. The main risks are getting the hypotheses stated so that the mapping to the 2010–2011 exchange is accepted, and the partial-regression algebra being fiddlier than expected. The repo already records the regression form as proved, which suggests the ground is prepared. The 30-day number is slightly below the best approach product on purpose: the exact Moran sign witness covers only the counterexample, while acceptance needs all three readings formalized in Lean plus the mapping.

approaches.note: Price and the 2x2 least-squares decomposition are short finite identities, and the mapping table is prose.
An explicit synergistic counterexample is a concrete rational computation that Lean can check by norm_num.
Broad phase maps across many model classes are a lot of simulation, and the boundary may be graded rather than sharp.
Same taxonomy as other formal routes, with the probability-space framing adding modest overhead.
Exact enumeration for N up to 8 is cheap, but the decision-tree mining of minimal assumption sets is loosely defined.
Three theorems with disjoint hypotheses including transmission bias; a bit more scope than the minimal route.
A seven-state Moran chain in rational arithmetic is small and fully specified, so the sign witness is very likely to be produced.
The stationary distribution is easy to compute, but whether the 0.05 gap appears depends on the chosen parameters.

problems.rationale: The acceptance criteria need a rigorous computer-assisted classification of all attractors of the cylindrical Douady–Couder map, including Lucas, over a stated parameter range; that requires validated-numerics infrastructure for a discontinuous placement rule that the swarm does not have. Simulation basin atlases and the static continued-fraction lattice theorems are tractable and will probably appear, but they do not meet the criteria on their own. A working interval-Newton certification of even the Fibonacci branch on a parameter interval would move me. The 30-day number is below the best approach product on purpose: the static lattice theorem and simulation atlases settle pieces but do not give the rigorous attractor classification the criteria require.

approaches.note: Conley–Morse covering of the front map's state space is heavy validated-numerics work, and the disc stays out of scope.
Mathlib has continued fractions, but formalizing visible parastichy pairs and the lattice-transition geometry is substantial.
Simulation is easy and sunflower count data are referenced by repo tests, but one-noise-parameter fits may come out ambiguous.
Exponential tail bounds plus box covering to 10^-6 uncovered measure is a long-shot validated-numerics project.
A pre-registered Monte Carlo basin atlas is routine and its thresholds give a definite outcome, though not a proof.
Interval Newton on a grid is doable for smooth branches, but grid points do not certify the whole interval and the map's discontinuities complicate it.
A long real-analysis paper is unlikely to be fully formalized in a month, as the proposer says.
Small disc simulations are cheap; the 0.01 unclassified-mass criterion gives a definite pass or fail.

problems.rationale: The acceptance criteria are a pre-registered test plus a verdict on linked selection, which the swarm can do from open Leffler and Buffalo supplements and GBIF ranges; the slope test itself will almost certainly reject neutral scaling. The blocker is the linked-selection half: published recombination maps exist for few of the compiled species, so the verdict may come out underpowered rather than definite. A logged slope test plus a recombination-covariate test on enough species would likely satisfy the criteria. The 30-day number is below the best approach product on purpose: the slope test alone gives no verdict on linked selection, which the criteria also require.

approaches.note: Assembling GBIF ranges, Damuth densities and a dated tree for 100+ species is several days of data work, and the H1 subset may be small.
Pedigree mutation rates exist for dozens of vertebrates, but matching them to π and census proxies yields a small, noisy sample.
SLiM ladders to 10^7 are compute-heavy, and the bound relies on analytic extrapolation the reviewers may contest.
Needs functional density and recombination covariates for 150 species, which are sparse outside model organisms.
Harmonized within-genome callsets and maps for 20 species are not readily available to agents.
Uses only published supplement columns and GBIF, and an interval excluding a slope of 1 is very likely given the known flatness.
Finding eight or more species with qualifying genetic maps is plausible, but the test is designed to return underpowered.
Generic forward simulations are feasible at moderate N, but spanning the empirical census range requires rescaling that weakens the comparison.

problems.rationale: Both acceptance routes are tractable: a pre-registered mammal PGLS on PanTHERIA/AnAge with model comparison will give one of the named verdicts, and the WBE derivation is a geometric-series argument that Lean handles easily. The main risks are data-cleaning choices (basal criteria, temperature joins) and whether reviewers accept the verdict as meeting the criteria rather than as 'underdetermined'; the curved or clade-specific model will very likely win. A logged PGLS result or a WBE Lean report would push this above 0.9.

approaches.note: Open data and standard PGLS tools; the temperature-corrected arm needs an AnAge join that may fall short of 300 species.
Finite geometric sums and a limit under named hypotheses are well within current Lean automation.
Depends on obtaining the DeLong et al. compilation in usable form, which the slice does not confirm.
Adding birds and leave-one-family-out ELPD is more work, but the decision rule always yields a heterogeneity verdict.
Countermodels for each weakened hypothesis add scope beyond the basic derivation.
Column-level specification of PanTHERIA and 100 Upham trees makes this nearly mechanical.
Standard WBE derivation plus one alternative lemma; the critique lemma's statement is the only fuzzy part.
A small deterministic network computation; settles convergence speed though it may reach 0.01 of 3/4 slowly.
